3. Plaintiffs' case in title suit no.37 of 1985 is that Abdul Gani Khalifa was the original owner of the suit land on whose death, Sk. Jummon, Mohiuddin, Idu, Karim, Joygun Bibi and Belaton Bibi became the owners of the suit land. The said Abdul Gani Khalifa settled the suit land in favour of Abdul Hakim, the predecessor of the plaintiffs on yearly rental basis, who constructed a dwelling house on the suit land. After the death of Abdul Gani Khalifa, Abdul Hakim executed a kabuliyat in Chaitra, 1348 B.S. in favour of said Sk. Jummon and others for a period of 11 years. Abdul Hakim mutated his name in the Municipal holding, paid rent to the Municipality and also paid rent to the Government and continued such possession till the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950, came into operation. In 1955 Abdul Hakim died and the plaintiffs continue such possession as of right. On 8.2.84, the defendants served a. notice upon them under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act demanding them to vacate possession of the suit land, which cast cloud in their title in the suit land. 

 8. It is admitted by the parties that Abdul Gani Khalifa was the original owner of the suit land who granted settlement of the suit land in favour of Abdul Hakim. It is also admitted fact that after the death of Abdul Gani Khalifa, Abdul Hakim executed a registered kabuliyat on 8th Chaitra, 1348 B. S. in favour of Sk. Jummon and others binding himself as tenant to pay yearly rent of Tk.3/= for 11 years in respect of the suit land. In the plaint there is positive averments that Abdul Hakim took settlement of the suit land and .thereafter he raised constructions in the suit land. In the written statement, the defendants have not denied the said facts, rather in paragraph 13(kha), they have admitted that Abdul Hakim gave lease of the land and not the premises with land. In such admitted position of the case, there is no dispute that Abdul Gani Khalifa gave lease of non-agricultural land to Abdul Hakim and the plaintiffs Predecessor Abdul Hakim was non-agricultural tenant within the meaning of Sub-section(5) of Section 2 of the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949, which provides: 

 In the plaint there is clear averment to the effect that the land was settled in favour of Abdul Hakim by Abdul Gani Khalifa. On a perusal of the said Kabuliyat ext 2, there is no dispute that the plaintiffs' predecessor was given "Miras settlement" of non-agricultural land for 11 years from before 22.3.42. Before the expiry of said period of 11 years, the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act 1949 came into force on 20th October 1949. It is an admitted fact that the "Miras settlement" of the suit land was granted at an annual rental of Tk.3/-. 

 10. The tenancy of Abdul Hakim was created under the provisions of the Bengal Non Agricultural Tenancy (Temporary Provisions) Act 1940, which tenancy was neither heritable nor transferable. The said Act, 1940 was repealed on 20.10.49 and the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act 1949 came into force on and from that date. Though the defendants claim that the plaintiffs surrendered possession, but they failed to prove such claim, rather it has been established from the pleadings as well as from the evidence on record that from before the date of execution of the kubutiyat, ext-2. Abdul Hakim had been in possession of the suit land in the same capacity for more than 12 years. Rights of a tenant of Non-Agricultural land were recognised under section 7 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, the relevant provision runs thus:- 

 (2) if the non-agricultural land comprised in any tenancy which has been or is created after the commencement of the Transfer of Property Act; 1882 (IV of 1882), has been held for a period of not less than twelve years without any lease in writing, or 

 (i) the tenant holding the non-agricultural land comprised in such tenancy shall not be ejected by his landlord from such land except on the ground that he has used such land in a manner which renders it unfit for use for any of the purposes specified in section 4; 

 (ii) subject to the provisions of section 91 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, (E.B. Act XXVIII of 1951), the interest of the tenant in the non-agricultural land comprised in such tenancy shall, in the case where such tenant dies intestate in respect of such interest, be transmitted by inheritance in the same manner as his other immovable property. 

 11. In view of the nature of settlement as given to Abdul Hakim "Mirash Bandubasta" of the suit land, followed by continuous possession over 12 years, by raising constructions such settlement, falls into one such class under section 7(2) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. The tenancy in question was created prior to 22.3.42 which continued on 20.10.49 when Act XXIII of 1949 came into force and in view of section 89A of the said Act, the plaintiffs acquired an interest to continue such possession as of right which is protected from eviction. The interest of Abdul Hakim in the suit land in such tenancy has been transmitted by inheritance to the plaintiffs on the death of Abdul Hakim under clause (II) of sub-section (5) of Section 7. 

 13. The Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act was amended by Ordinance No. IX of 1967, wherein certain chapters and sections of the said Act were repealed and section 26A was inserted prohibiting sub-letting of tenancy, which provides:- 

 "26A(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or in any other law for the time being in force or in any contract, no non-agricultural tenant shall sub-let the whole or any part of his tenancy on any terms or conditions whatsoever. 

 (2) If any tenancy or any part of a tenancy is sub-let, in contravention of the provision of sub-section(1), the interest of the non-agricultural tenant in the tenancy or in that part of the tenancy, as the case may be, shall be extinguished, and the tenancy or the part of the tenancy shall vest in the Government from the date of such sub-letting free from all encumbrances. 

 " This provision is almost similar to section 75A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. The intention of the legislature in inserting this provision and deletion of certain provisions is clear. The rights of the landlord of non-agricultural land which they had, even after the acquisition of rent receiving interest has been curtailed, on and from the date of promulgation of ordinance No. IX of 1967. There cannot be any new lease of non-agricultural land from the date of promulgation of the said ordinance. The expression "subletting" connotes the creation of a sub-ordinate tenancy or under raiyat, under which the sub-lessee would but for a special contract be liable to pay rent for that land to a person other than the Government. The purpose of inserting this section appears to be that since after the acquisition of the interest of rent receivers by the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, the rent receivers were themselves to retain certain classes of retainable khas land as tenants directly under the Government, they should not be allowed to create further sub-tenancies under them. I am therefore, of the view that the plaintiffs status became tenants under th6 Government after section 26A, came into force. Considering this aspect of the matter, Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan finds difficult to oppose the rule. He however, feebly argues that the court of appeal below was justified in dismissing the suit. 

 15. The court of appeal below misconstrued Ext. 2, the kabuliyat and held that the said deed being an unilateral deed," Abdul Hakim was a lessee under the defendants and not tenant in the suit land and that as no bilateral lease deed was executed, the said kabuliyat is hit by section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act. The court of appeal below further held that Abdul Hakim was not a yearly tenant, who acquired no status as "tenant" under the Non-agricultural Tenancy Act. The court of appeal below totally misread ext.2 wherein there is specific recitals to the effect that the tenancy would be heritable, which was created at a yearly rental of Tk.3/=. The court of appeal below also did not consider section 7 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, under which provision if the landlord allows the tenant to erect pucca structures in the tenanted land such tenancy will be heritable. It may be pointed out here that Abdul Hakim raised construction in the suit land is not disputed by the defendants. In view of such facts, though the suit land was recorded in the name of the defendants, I am of the opinion that such record will not stand on the way in getting a decree by the plaintiffs in the suit since the plaintiffs have acquired a heritable, non-eject able right in the suit land particularly when the said S.A. record which was prepared after 1960, after the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act 1949 came into force. I am further of the view that the plaintiffs have acquired a right which cannot be said anything less than title in the suit land. The court of appeal below upon misconstruction of Ext. 2, the Kabuliyat held that Abdul Hakim was given lease of the suit land by Kabuliyat ext.2 which is hit by section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act. This decision of the court of appeal below is an error occasioning failure of justice In that view of the matter, the learned Assistant Judge was justified in finding title of the plaintiffs in the suit land and has rightly decreed the suit.
